questions.question_text: Which graph is best for displaying the distribution of a single quantitative variable?
questions.option_b: a histogram
questions.explanation: Histograms show the shape, center, and spread of quantitative data using bins. Bar charts and pie charts display CATEGORICAL data; two-way tables show relationships between two categorical variables.

questions.question_text: In a boxplot, an outlier is typically a value beyond:
questions.option_b: 1.5 × IQR above Q3 or below Q1
questions.explanation: The 1.5 × IQR rule flags outliers past Q1 − 1.5·IQR or Q3 + 1.5·IQR. This is resistant to extreme values, unlike standard-deviation-based rules that the outliers themselves distort.

questions.question_text: If a distribution is roughly symmetric, the mean and median will be:
questions.option_b: approximately equal
questions.explanation: Symmetry pulls the mean toward the median. In right skew the mean exceeds the median; in left skew it's below. Comparing mean and median is a quick skewness check.

questions.question_text: Multiplying every data value by 3 changes the standard deviation by a factor of:
questions.explanation: Multiplying by a constant scales the SD by that constant (×3), and the variance by its square (×9). Adding a constant, by contrast, leaves spread unchanged.

questions.question_text: A residual plot with a clear curved pattern suggests:
questions.option_b: a linear model is NOT appropriate for the data
questions.explanation: A good linear fit produces residuals scattered randomly around zero. A curved pattern means the relationship is nonlinear, so a line is the wrong model — reading the residual plot is essential.

questions.question_text: Correlation coefficient r ranges from:
questions.option_b: −1 to 1
questions.explanation: r runs from −1 (perfect negative) through 0 (no linear association) to +1 (perfect positive). Its sign gives direction and its magnitude gives strength of the LINEAR relationship.

questions.question_text: An influential point in regression is one that:
questions.option_b: substantially changes the slope or correlation if removed
questions.explanation: Influential points (often high-leverage x-values) pull the regression line toward themselves; removing them noticeably changes the fit. Not every outlier is influential — leverage matters.

questions.question_text: Blinding in an experiment means that:
questions.option_a: subjects are kept in the dark
questions.option_b: subjects and/or evaluators don't know who received which treatment
questions.explanation: Blinding prevents expectations from biasing results; double-blinding hides treatment from both subjects and assessors. It controls the placebo effect and observer bias — distinct from randomization.

questions.question_text: A confounding variable is one that:
questions.option_a: is the same as the response variable
questions.option_b: is associated with both the explanatory variable and the response, distorting the relationship
questions.explanation: A confounder is tangled with the explanatory variable so you can't separate their effects on the response. Random assignment balances confounders across groups, which is why experiments support causation.

questions.question_text: The purpose of replication (many subjects per treatment) in an experiment is to:
questions.option_b: reduce the role of chance variation and reveal real treatment effects
questions.explanation: More subjects average out individual variability, making genuine treatment differences detectable. Replication (along with control and randomization) is a pillar of good experimental design.

questions.question_text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). The subtraction is needed to:
questions.option_b: avoid double-counting the overlap of A and B
questions.explanation: The general addition rule subtracts the intersection so outcomes in both A and B aren't counted twice. For mutually exclusive events the overlap is 0, simplifying to P(A) + P(B).

questions.question_text: The expected value of a discrete random variable is:
questions.option_b: the long-run average, found by summing each value times its probability
questions.explanation: E(X) = Σ[x · P(x)] is the probability-weighted mean — the average over many trials. It need not equal any single possible outcome (e.g., an expected 2.5 children).

questions.question_text: For independent X and Y, the mean of X + Y equals:
questions.option_b: E(X) + E(Y)
questions.explanation: Means always add for sums (E(X+Y) = E(X) + E(Y)), independence or not. Independence matters for VARIANCES (which add for both sums and differences), not for combining means.

questions.question_text: As sample size increases, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄:
questions.option_b: decreases (as σ/√n)
questions.explanation: The standard error σ/√n shrinks as n grows, so larger samples give more precise estimates of the mean. This is why bigger samples produce narrower confidence intervals.

questions.question_text: A statistic is an unbiased estimator of a parameter if:
questions.option_b: its sampling distribution is centered at the true parameter value
questions.explanation: Unbiased means the estimator's expected value equals the parameter — on average it hits the target, though any single estimate may miss. The sample mean and sample proportion are unbiased estimators.

questions.question_text: Which condition checks that the sampling distribution of p̂ is approximately normal?
questions.explanation: The large-counts condition requires at least 10 successes and 10 failures. The n ≥ 30 rule applies to MEANS via the CLT; each parameter has its own normality condition.

questions.question_text: Increasing the confidence level from 90% to 99% (same data) makes the interval:
questions.option_b: wider
questions.explanation: Higher confidence requires capturing the parameter more often, so the interval must be wider (larger critical value). There's a trade-off: more confidence means less precision for fixed n.

questions.question_text: Degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-test with n = 20 is:
questions.explanation: For a one-sample t procedure, df = n − 1 = 19. The −1 reflects estimating the population SD from the sample, which uses up one degree of freedom.

questions.question_text: A 95% confidence interval for a difference of means that contains 0 indicates:
questions.option_b: no statistically significant difference at the 0.05 level
questions.explanation: If 0 is a plausible difference, you can't reject 'no difference' at α = 0.05. It doesn't PROVE the means are equal — it just means the evidence for a difference is insufficient.

questions.question_text: Decreasing the significance level α from 0.05 to 0.01 makes a Type I error:
questions.option_b: less likely
questions.option_d: equal to a Type II error
questions.explanation: α IS the probability of a Type I error (rejecting a true H₀), so lowering it reduces that risk — but it raises the chance of a Type II error and lowers power. The two errors trade off.

questions.question_text: In a chi-square test, the expected count for each cell is calculated as:
questions.option_b: (row total × column total) / grand total
questions.explanation: Expected counts under independence = (row total × column total)/grand total. The chi-square statistic then sums (observed − expected)²/expected across cells.

questions.question_text: A large chi-square test statistic generally leads to:
questions.option_a: a large P-value and failing to reject H₀
questions.option_b: a small P-value and evidence against H₀
questions.explanation: A large χ² means observed counts differ greatly from expected, producing a small P-value and evidence against the null (independence/goodness-of-fit). Big test statistic → small P-value is the general pattern.

questions.question_text: The standard error of the slope in regression measures:
questions.option_b: the variability of the estimated slope across repeated samples
questions.explanation: The slope's standard error quantifies how much the estimated slope would vary from sample to sample. It's the denominator of the t-statistic used to test whether the true slope is 0.

questions.question_text: Which condition is NOT required for inference about a regression slope?
questions.option_b: the explanatory variable is categorical
questions.explanation: Regression inference assumes Linearity, Independence, Normality of residuals, and Equal variance (LINE) — with a QUANTITATIVE explanatory variable. A categorical predictor isn't a regression-slope condition.

questions.question_text: The interquartile range (IQR) is:
questions.option_b: Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of data
questions.explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1 captures the middle half of the data and resists outliers, unlike the range (max − min). It's the spread measure paired with the median for skewed data.

questions.question_text: Two events are mutually exclusive (disjoint) if they:
questions.option_b: cannot occur at the same time, so P(A and B) = 0
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events share no outcomes (P(A and B) = 0). They are NOT independent — if A happens, B definitely didn't, so knowing one affects the other. The exam loves this distinction.

questions.question_text: The Central Limit Theorem says that for large n, the sampling distribution of x̄ is approximately normal:
questions.option_a: only if the population is normal
questions.option_b: regardless of the population's shape
questions.explanation: The CLT's power is that x̄ becomes approximately normal for large enough n EVEN when the population is skewed. This is what makes inference about means broadly possible.

questions.question_text: The margin of error in a confidence interval depends on the critical value, the standard error, and:
questions.option_b: is fully determined by those two — larger n shrinks the standard error
questions.explanation: Margin of error = critical value × standard error. Larger samples reduce the standard error (∝ 1/√n), shrinking the margin. Population size barely matters when it's much larger than the sample.
